title: Affordable housing policy and tax exemption
subtitle: Reaching Home funding, tenant protections, land for housing, and paramedic response times and code changes.
overview: The Community and Health Services Committee spent most of the afternoon on the "Homes for All" package. It recommended that staff explore ways to preserve existing affordable housing, including a multi-unit rental acquisition program, right of first refusal policies and a regional housing needs assessment. It also recommended work on protections against renovation, conversion and demolition evictions, and advocacy to the federal and provincial governments for acquisition programs.

The committee also recommended a property tax exemption program for affordable housing. Regional and education taxes could be exempted for housing providers who keep rents affordable. Staff said the exemption does not change the levy but slightly shrinks the assessment base, so other properties would carry a fractionally higher rate. Council must still adopt these recommendations.

The committee recommended adding $1,542,836 in Reaching Home funding to the 2024 homelessness budget with no net tax levy impact. It received for information reports on land for affordable housing, the 2023 food safety program, seniors dental care and paramedic service performance. Paramedic staff signalled plans to rename the "Code Red" and "Code Yellow" system statuses and to propose new response time targets later this year.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended increasing the 2024 Homelessness and Supportive Housing operating budget by $1,542,836, matched by federal subsidy, with no net property tax levy impact.

The committee recommended directing staff to explore a Multi-Unit Rental Acquisition Program and right of first refusal policies, and to work with area municipalities to assemble a regional housing needs assessment {{vote:m4}}.

The committee recommended that staff work with area municipalities on renovation, conversion and demolition protection policies, and with service providers to identify gaps in support for displaced tenants {{vote:m5}}.

The committee recommended asking the federal and Ontario governments to create programs supporting the acquisition and conversion of private market properties into permanent affordable and supportive homes {{vote:m6}}.

decisions.item: Property tax exemption for affordable housing
decisions.detail: The committee recommended replacing the existing by-law, approving the exemption program and guidelines, and having staff develop applications for Q2 2024, work with area municipalities, and advocate on the Ontario Trillium Benefit {{vote:m7}}.

debate: Delegates from tenant, co-operative and housing groups supported the proposals. They described renovation-related evictions, a lack of affordable units to move to, and the need to protect existing affordable housing as well as build new.

A delegate from a community housing co-operative argued the tax exemption would help non-profits compete with large investors for older apartment buildings. They said it should affect few properties because of long affordability commitments.

Councillors asked who bears the cost. Staff said the levy does not change, but taxes not paid by exempt properties are ultimately spread across other properties through a slightly smaller assessment base.

Some councillors worried about duplicating work in area municipalities, particularly the needs assessment, and about limited early engagement with them. Staff changed "create" to "assemble" to clarify the region would pull together existing work.

Councillors raised that tenants in exempt buildings could lose Ontario Trillium Benefit eligibility. Staff acknowledged this and proposed advocacy to the province. Councillors also questioned right of first refusal, which staff said needs provincial enabling legislation.
